title: What is shared
hookLine: one Allah, one Prophet ﷺ, one Qur'an, one qiblah, five prayers

lines: ONE GOD. ONE PROPHET. ONE QUR'AN.
cards: Try a short list. One God. One Prophet, Muhammad ﷺ.
One Qur'an, the same words in the same order. One direction to face, the Kaaba in Mecca. Prayer, day and night, bowing and putting the forehead to the ground.
The fast of Ramadan. The pilgrimage to the same house, walking around it in the same direction. That list is true for a Sunni Muslim in one city and a Shia Muslim in another.
After a long look at a split, here is the other column. Today: what is shared.

teach.h: PRAY OUR PRAYER, FACE OUR QIBLAH.
teach.b: A hadith in al-Bukhari draws the line with almost nothing.
The Prophet said, in effect: whoever prays our prayer, faces our qiblah, and eats what we slaughter, that one is a Muslim, under the protection of God and His Messenger.
Three plain, outward things: a prayer, a direction, a meal. That is the whole measure this report gives.

teach.h: HOLD FAST TO THE ROPE TOGETHER.
teach.b: Then the Qur'an: "And hold fast, all of you together, to the cable of Allah, and do not separate." A rope, held by many hands. The verse doesn't ask everyone to stand in the same spot on the rope.
It asks them to keep holding it. Now the qiblah, the direction you face.
Muslims in prayer turn toward the same house, so the rows of the whole world, seen from above, would form rings around one center. Sunni and Shia alike. Even the differences sit inside the shared.
Both pray the five daily prayers; Shia practice allows gathering them into three times of day, and Sunni schools allow joining them in certain cases, such as travel.
Tomorrow looks at the smaller differences you can see in a row of worshipers; they too sit inside one prayer, facing one way. The split was real, and the grief was real.
But set the two lists side by side, and see which one runs longer.

how: Sunni and Shia Muslims share the Qur'an, the five daily prayers facing the Kaaba, the Ramadan fast and the pilgrimage to Mecca; differences such as hand position or combining prayer times sit within that shared practice.

o: the direction faced in prayer, toward the Kaaba
the call to prayer sung from the minaret
the niche in a mosque wall where the imam stands

games.q: what is shared — tap the pairs.
p: the direction you face in prayer
hold fast together to the rope
prays our prayer, faces our qiblah

s: Sunni and Shia Muslims face different directions in prayer
both face the same qiblah, the Kaaba in Mecca.
a hadith names outward things, like praying and facing the qiblah, as the mark of a Muslim
whoever prays our prayer, faces our qiblah and eats what we slaughter, the hadith says.
Shia Muslims pray only three prayers a day
they pray the five; Shia practice allows gathering them into three times of day.

games.q: someone asks the Prophet's measure for who counts as a Muslim. which answer does the hadith give?
o: whoever agrees with us about every question.
whoever prays our prayer, faces our qiblah and eats what we slaughter.
whoever was born in our tribe.
games.why: the hadith in al-Bukhari gives three plain, outward signs, and places that person under the protection of God and His Messenger.

practice: If you are Muslim, count on your fingers, one item per breath, what you share with every Muslim: God, the Prophet, the Qur'an, the qiblah, the prayer, the fast, the pilgrimage.
If you're not, make the same kind of list with someone you differ from, what you both love, fear and hope for, and let it grow longer than you expected.

wordCard.voice: Qiblah, the direction faced in prayer: toward the Kaaba, the same for Sunni and Shia Muslims, alongside one God, one Prophet, one Qur'an, and one prayer. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the direction faced in prayer, toward the Kaaba, faced by Sunni and Shia alike.

carryVoice: Your line: more shared than split. Every row on earth bends around one center. Nine hundred days now.
